input:
Moving returned goods back through the supply chain is easy to overlook, yet it accumulates a substantial cost over a year. This review sets out to establish, on a firm evidential footing, exactly what the plant's returns flow costs in carrier transport.

The review draws exclusively on the plant's own records. The costs in question are the carrier invoices for the last 12 months, and no estimates, allocations, or apportionments have been introduced at any stage. The pattern of operation is straightforward: the returns flow runs 128 km per trip, the carrier charges a rate of $1.7 per km, and over the year the flow made a total of 857 trips. It is particularly important to note that empty running is included in this trip count, which means the figure represents the full cost of the flow as operated, rather than merely the cost of the loaded journeys. Multiplying the distance by the rate gives a cost per trip of $217.6, and it is this per-trip figure, carried over the year's trips, that builds up into the annual total.

Bringing all of these elements together, the returns flow costs $186k a year in carrier transport. Because the annual figure is the product of the trip length, the rate per kilometre, and the number of trips, it moves in direct proportion to any change in those quantities, underpinned throughout by the invoice record. In summary, the review establishes the annual cost of the returns flow at $186k, on a fully recorded basis, with empty running firmly inside the trip count.
target:
The returns flow costs $186k a year in carrier transport. The figure is the full cost of the flow as operated: empty running is included in it, not added to it.

The annual cost is the product of three recorded quantities. The flow runs 128 km per trip, the carrier charges $1.7 per km, and the flow makes 857 trips per year. The cost per trip is $217.6, and the annual total is the per-trip cost carried over the year's trips. Each quantity in the product is a record, not an estimate: the costs are carrier invoices for the last 12 months, and the trip count is the count of trips actually run, loaded and empty together. No allocation or apportionment enters the figure; each invoice belongs to a trip the flow made.

The per-trip figure is the working number of the review. It prices a single return movement at the recorded distance and the recorded rate, and it is the figure against which a change in the flow is costed: a change in trip length reprices every trip, and a change in the trip count scales the annual total in direct proportion. The annual figure moves with exactly the quantities that compose it and with nothing else.

The review closes on the recorded position. The returns flow costs $186k a year, established from carrier invoices, with empty running inside the trip count.
